profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting at a large software company that is evaluating whether to build a new advanced code-analysis capability on top of Desyan for its internal secure-development platform. The context is that the company already runs fast Soufflé-style value-flow checks in CI, but several teams want better reasoning about configuration-dependent bugs and security conditions without paying the cost of full symbolic execution everywhere. The agenda is to brainstorm what a first Desyan-based initiative should look like, what kind of pilot would be realistic for Q3, how to describe the technical story around path sensitivity and symbolic fallback, and what evidence would make the effort credible internally. The expected outcome is a shortlist of 2-3 candidate pilot ideas plus a rough framing for how the team will position the effort to leadership and potential early adopters.

members.name: Nisha Rao
members.expertise: Program analysis, Datalog engines, points-to/data-flow analysis, Soufflé-based tooling, research-to-production transfer
members.background: Nisha joined from a programming-languages research lab and has spent the last three years modernizing the company's internal static-analysis stack for scale and incremental analysis.
members.private_state: She wants the Desyan effort to stay technically credible and low-risk, with room to validate the integration architecture before anyone treats it as a user-facing product commitment.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' should primarily be a shadow evaluation and internal prototype run by the analysis team, not something exposed directly to application teams in their normal CI workflow.
When people say 'real-world benchmark set,' they usually mean the internally mirrored corpus of open-source Java and C++ apps already used for performance and precision regression testing.
In this context, 'path-sensitive' naturally means lightweight intraprocedural branch refinement using Desyan's Datalog-native symbolic reasoning, with only selective escalation beyond that.
A 'symbolic fallback' is something the engine does in batch after value-flow saturation identifies ambiguous cases, not an interactive or per-finding user-facing capability.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.expertise: Developer tooling, CI/CD integration, internal platform adoption, security scan workflows, productizing infrastructure
members.background: Leo leads the platform layer that delivers build-time quality and security checks to product teams, and he has a history of turning promising infrastructure into narrowly scoped but visible internal launches.
members.private_state: He needs a story that leadership can see in action within a quarter and that a couple of partner teams can try without needing a research-heavy setup.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' normally means a limited but real rollout to one or two partner engineering teams inside their existing CI or code-review flow.
When someone mentions 'real-world repos,' the useful interpretation is live internal services with authentic build complexity, generated code, and deployment-specific configuration behavior.

For a new analysis to be described as 'path-sensitive' in a compelling way, it should follow meaningful conditions across function boundaries and common request-handling flows, not just inside a single procedure.
If the platform mentions 'symbolic fallback,' teams will expect it to support on-demand drill-down for specific findings or reruns, so analysts can explain why a warning is real.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the Q3 pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss doing a 'Q3 pilot' and sound aligned on moving quickly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the pilot is an internal, analysis-team-run shadow experiment that compares Desyan-enabled checks against existing pipelines without exposing results to end users.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the pilot is a small live rollout to a couple of product teams, with findings surfaced in the normal developer workflow.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both interpretations plausibly fit the word 'pilot' in engineering organizations, and brainstorming meetings often intentionally leave rollout details fuzzy, so the phrase creates false consensus instead of triggering clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to validating ideas on the 'real-world benchmark set' or 'real-world repos.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the company's established internal benchmark corpus: mirrored open-source projects and regression fixtures that are operationally convenient but still non-production.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of two active internal services owned by partner teams, with genuine dependency graphs, build flakes, and organization-specific code patterns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The organization already has multiple artifacts that are casually described as 'real-world,' and each person works with a different default set often enough that the phrase feels perfectly ordinary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both like the idea of a 'path-sensitive mode' for the first Desyan-backed analysis.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a bounded, mainly intraprocedural mode where simple path predicates are handled natively in Datalog and only narrow ambiguity remains.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a mode that preserves conditions through common call chains or request-processing flows well enough to noticeably reduce noisy alerts in service code.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are using the same established technical term, and neither interpretation is obviously wrong; in early brainstorming, the term sounds precise enough even though each person silently assumes a different practical scope.

misalignment_points.topic: How symbolic fallback will be used
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the analysis can rely on 'symbolic fallback' or 'solver fallback' when value-flow reasoning is not enough.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes fallback is an offline engine behavior: after fixpoint, the analysis batches ambiguous tuples and invokes SMT selectively during the computation pipeline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes fallback is a workflow behavior: when a finding needs explanation, the system can invoke deeper symbolic reasoning on demand for that case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the high-level purpose and both know Desyan can combine Datalog and SMT, so the unresolved question of when and where the solver is invoked sounds like an implementation detail not worth pausing on during ideation.

turns.inner_thought: Desyan is interesting precisely because we can test whether the Datalog-plus-SMT integration holds up without overcommitting. If we keep the Q3 pilot as an analysis-team-run shadow exercise, we can compare against the current Soufflé-style checks, study cost and precision, and avoid creating expectations with product teams before the architecture is proven.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I wanted to use this session to pressure-test what a first Desyan-based effort could look like. At a high level, it gives us a way to blend the fast value-flow machinery we already trust with more selective symbolic reasoning, so the question is what a focused Q3 pilot should be.

turns.inner_thought: If this lands in Q3, it has to be something leadership can actually see in the platform, even if it's narrow. A pilot that never reaches a couple of partner teams won't count as momentum. I need a version that fits into normal CI or review and doesn't require a research-style operating model.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that makes sense to me. A Q3 pilot is realistic if we keep the scope tight and make sure it shows up in the existing developer-tooling experience in a way a couple of partner teams can understand without a huge setup.

turns.inner_thought: Best starting point is a current security analysis where we already know the baseline. Path-sensitive mode, in my mind, means bounded branch refinement inside procedures with Desyan's native symbolic predicates, maybe escalating only in a few cases. That should preserve throughput and keep implementation risk under control.
turns.utterance: One place to start would be to take an analysis we already run today and add a path-sensitive mode to it. That would let us keep the Soufflé-scale throughput story while getting smarter about branch conditions in the cases where the current checks flatten too much.

turns.inner_thought: If we say path-sensitive mode, I want it to mean something service teams will immediately feel: fewer bogus alerts because the analysis carries meaningful conditions through the request path, not just inside one local block. Otherwise it'll sound like a technical refinement with no visible developer benefit.
turns.utterance: I like that framing. From the platform side, path-sensitive mode gets compelling when it follows request-flow conditions far enough to actually clean up the noisy findings teams already complain about. If we can tell that story, people will immediately get why it matters.

turns.inner_thought: Before anything else, we should run on the internal benchmark corpus we already use for regression: mirrored open-source Java and C++ apps, stable fixtures, easy apples-to-apples comparisons. That's the fastest way to see whether the Desyan integration is real or just a demo.
turns.utterance: Before we get too attached to one idea, I'd want to validate candidate analyses on the real-world benchmark set we already use. That gives us a quick comparison point against the current engine on both performance and precision, and it helps separate architectural promise from wishful thinking.

turns.inner_thought: Benchmarks are fine, but for credibility I really need two live internal services with all the ugly build behavior and org-specific patterns. Leadership won't be moved by curated repos alone. If it survives real-world repos from partner teams, then we have a launch story.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I also think it helps if we can talk about real-world repos, because leadership tends to trust examples that survive actual build complexity. If we can anchor the story there too, it becomes much easier to position.

turns.inner_thought: The clean architecture is: saturate value flow first, keep as much reasoning as possible in Datalog, then batch the ambiguous cases and invoke SMT selectively. Symbolic fallback should be rare, offline, and controlled by the engine, not something in the workflow that explodes costs or expectations.
turns.utterance: On architecture, my bias would be to keep the common path in native reasoning and rely on symbolic fallback only when value-flow alone can't resolve the remaining ambiguity. That keeps the fast path simple and gives us a principled way to spend extra compute where it buys us something.

turns.inner_thought: That's good, and if we mention symbolic fallback, I want to be able to tell teams they can drill into a finding when they need to explain it. The key benefit isn't just backend cleverness; it's avoiding global cost while still giving reviewers an on-demand deeper pass on the few alerts they care about.
turns.utterance: Right, and symbolic fallback is especially attractive if it means we don't pay that cost everywhere. For the few findings people actually care about, having that deeper check available would make the overall workflow much easier to defend.

turns.inner_thought: We should keep the candidate set tight: maybe config-dependent taint or path-aware nullability. Both are implementable without blowing up the engine. And both can fit a pilot if it's just the analysis team evaluating on our benchmark corpus plus some internal comparisons. The taint one is likely cleaner for demonstrating conditional reasoning.
turns.utterance: To narrow it down, I think we probably have two credible candidates for a first pass: a config-dependent taint check, or a path-aware nullability analysis. Either one could support a pilot with modest engineering overhead, and both give us a clean way to talk about value flow plus a path-sensitive mode.

turns.inner_thought: Config-dependent taint is easier to explain to partner teams: 'this warning only matters under certain config paths' is concrete. And for adoption, I need examples from actual internal services, not just benchmark graphs. If we can show that on real-world repos, it becomes a very legible platform story.
turns.utterance: My instinct is to lean toward the config-dependent taint idea. It's easier to explain, and the adoption story is stronger if we can pair it with credible examples from real-world repos. That feels like something partner teams would immediately understand.

turns.inner_thought: I'll write a concept note that frames this as extending the existing engine, not replacing it, and I'll line up benchmark experiments on the internal corpus. I also want comparison data for native reasoning versus solver fallback in the batch pipeline so we can quantify precision gain and cost before anyone asks for broader exposure.
turns.utterance: That works. That should give us something concrete to react to before we lock the shape of the effort.

turns.inner_thought: Great. Once I have her concept note, I'll package this as a small visible Q3 pilot and start lining up one or two early adopters so we can get it into their normal flow. If I can show leadership an actual trial with recognizable teams, this has a real chance of getting support.
